stem: Two speakers produce acoustically different versions of the same word. Listeners identify both correctly. What problem must a speech-perception account explain?
choices: Stable linguistic identity despite physical variation
Each speaker's voice establishes a separate word meaning
Only differences between identical physical tokens can be recognized
Recognition requires the listener to reproduce the speaker's acoustics
why: Speaker and context variation can preserve word identity. Recognition must tolerate that variation while retaining differences that distinguish words.

stem: A synthesis experiment changes vocal-tract resonance while holding the excitation source fixed. Which property is being manipulated most directly?
choices: The filter's formant pattern
The timing between consonant release and voicing
The source's fundamental repetition rate
The listener's decision boundary while acoustics remain fixed
why: Formants reflect resonances imposed by the tract. Holding the source constant isolates the filter's contribution to the resulting vowel.

stem: A vowel spectrogram shows several strong horizontal frequency bands. A student calls every band a separate syllable. What correction is needed?
choices: Several formants can belong to one vowel at the same time
Each band represents one successive phoneme
The bands primarily show syllable intensity rather than resonance
F1 and F2 name the first two syllables
why: Frequency bands can occur simultaneously within one vowel. A syllable sequence unfolds over time; formant number orders resonances by frequency.

stem: A synthetic /u/ has low F1 and low F2. If F2 is changed while the source remains constant, what comparison does the manipulation support?
choices: How resonance changes affect perceived vowel quality
How changing voicing onset affects a stop-consonant boundary
How source pitch changes while the filter remains fixed
How different natural speakers' many acoustic differences combine
why: The manipulation isolates a resonance change. It does not change vocabulary, introduce different speakers, or directly test production.

stem: Removing the estimated vocal-tract filter leaves a buzz-like signal. Why does applying another filter remain informative?
choices: The same source can be shaped into a different resonance pattern
The source retains the original resonance pattern unchanged
Applying a filter changes the listener's vocabulary directly
The procedure holds the output constant while changing its interpretation
why: Reusing the source permits a controlled comparison of filters. Synthesis manipulates physical causes; a separate perceptual response measures what is heard.

stem: Two vowel clouds overlap in an F1–F2 plot. Which conclusion fits the lecture?
choices: A single formant pair may not uniquely identify the vowel
Each vowel occupies one nonoverlapping acoustic point
Every overlapping token must be the same linguistic vowel
F2 can be ignored once F1 is measured accurately
why: Vowel space summarizes useful but variable distributions. Overlap makes recognition less like matching one invariant point, without making formants irrelevant.

stem: Why use synthesized /b/–/d/–/g/ transitions rather than only recordings of three different natural syllables?
choices: One acoustic dimension can vary while other properties are controlled
To guarantee identical discrimination before collecting responses
To compare naturally co-varying speaker and syllable properties
To replace the identification task with an acoustic measurement
why: Controlled transitions separate physical manipulation from perceptual response. Equal physical steps do not guarantee equal perceived differences.

stem: Stimuli differ in equal F2-onset steps. Pair A crosses a labeling boundary; pair B stays within a category at the same separation. Why compare them?
choices: To test category effects without confounding acoustic distance
To determine whether greater physical distance improves discrimination
To compare identification accuracy without a discrimination task
To locate the most frequent vowel in natural speech
why: Matching distance lets boundary position predict discrimination independently of the programmed step difference.

stem: A labeling task produces three peaked response regions because participants choose /b/, /d/, or /g/. Why is that alone insufficient for categorical perception?
choices: Discrete response options can produce categorical-looking labels
Any peaked identification curve necessarily proves information loss
The endpoints alone determine sensitivity in every interior pair
Discrimination is redundant once three labels are available
why: The response task requires categories. The classic argument also examines whether discrimination follows labeling boundaries for matched physical differences.

stem: A noncategorical observer is equally sensitive to equal F2 differences everywhere. What discrimination pattern is predicted?
choices: Roughly equal accuracy across equally separated pairs
Higher accuracy wherever the labeling curve changes fastest
Lower accuracy within a category despite equal physical spacing
Increasing accuracy only when a pair is assigned different labels
why: Uniform physical sensitivity predicts a flat matched-distance discrimination function. Boundary-linked peaks are the competing categorical prediction.

stem: Labeling changes sharply near two points, and matched-distance discrimination peaks near those same points. What is the strongest interpretation?
choices: Perceived similarity is organized by category boundaries
Only final labels matter; discrimination adds no independent evidence
The pattern identifies a uniquely human speech mechanism
The measured categories establish that no graded information survives
why: The joint pattern supports categorical perception. It does not specify every internal stage or establish developmental identity.

stem: Two listeners' category boundaries occur at different stimulus numbers. What analysis best preserves the theoretical comparison?
choices: Relate each discrimination peak to that listener's boundary
Use one fixed physical boundary for every participant
Compare group-average discrimination only with the endpoints
Treat a shifted boundary as failure to form any category
why: The prediction links discrimination to a listener's category organization. Misaligned individual boundaries can blur a group-average function.

stem: The abbreviated class discrimination task contains only physically different pairs. Why can a same response still be informative?
choices: It shows that a physical difference was not detected in that judgment
A same judgment establishes that the acoustic files matched
The design directly estimates the rate of correct same judgments
Any different response demonstrates equal sensitivity everywhere
why: All pairs differ physically, but some differences may not be perceived. A full same/different design would additionally assess response tendencies.

stem: Why might poorer discrimination within a category support useful speech recognition?
choices: It groups irrelevant token variation while preserving meaningful contrasts
It improves recognition by preserving every physical difference equally
It helps only if all within-category variation is deleted at every level
It stabilizes recognition by preventing sensitivity at boundaries
why: Category stability helps cope with variation. Sensitivity remains especially useful at contrasts that distinguish linguistic units.

stem: An infant's sucking declines during repeated sounds and rises after a new token. What does recovery primarily indicate?
choices: Detection of a stimulus change
Explicit knowledge of which word the sound begins
A demonstrated label change rather than only discrimination
A stable preference for one phoneme regardless of repetition
why: Habituation and recovery provide a behavioral discrimination measure. They do not require a verbal report or establish knowledge of words or syntax.

stem: Infants recover more sucking after a boundary-crossing change than after an equal within-category change. What result does this parallel?
choices: The relation between adult category boundaries and discrimination
Discrimination tracks acoustic spacing without category effects
Infants show mature lexical recognition of the syllables
Recovery proves all linguistic categories were innately specified
why: The response depends on category relationship, not only physical distance. Habituation is the starting state from which detection is measured.

stem: English-learning infants become less successful on a contrast used in Hindi but not English. Which interpretation fits perceptual narrowing?
choices: Experience increasingly tunes sensitivity toward native-language distinctions
A general age-related decrease in hearing acuity
A loss of all categorical organization after early infancy
Evidence that later infants have forgotten specific Hindi word meanings
why: The change is selective and language-related. It does not imply a general hearing decline or prove universal initial sensitivity.

stem: Adults show sharp labels and boundary-linked discrimination for plucked/bowed nonspeech sounds. Which claim is directly challenged?
choices: Categorical perception occurs only for speech
Categorical perception cannot be measured using labels
Categorical effects are absent in speech
Only experience-free categories can occur outside speech
why: Nonspeech categories challenge language exclusivity. They do not deny speech acoustics or the existence of categorical organization.

stem: Trained chinchillas produce categorical-like responses along a speech VOT continuum. What follows?
choices: Human language possession is not required for this perceptual pattern
The animals acquired the same lexical meanings as adults
Reward training proves that human phoneme categories require explicit rewards
Speech categories necessarily reflect a mechanism exclusive to language
why: The demonstrated response organization extends beyond humans. Categorizing speech sounds is not equivalent to possessing a language.

stem: A difficult nasal contrast becomes more detectable with relevant infant experience. How does this extend the narrowing account?
choices: Experience can strengthen distinctions as well as reduce unused ones
Learning only preserves distinctions already equally clear at birth
Age alone strengthens every contrast regardless of environment
Experience improves vocabulary but cannot change sound discrimination
why: The contrast's improvement supports experience-dependent acquisition. A complete developmental account includes both loss and gain in effective distinctions.

stem: Which observation most directly challenges a model that waits for completed phoneme decisions before beginning lexical processing?
choices: Within-category acoustic differences change lexical competition
Final identification selects one word rather than two
Listeners discriminate some cross-boundary sound pairs well
Acoustic features and words use different representations
why: A completed-symbol gate would discard the relevant within-category differences. Graded competitor effects show those differences influencing later processing.

stem: A strict phoneme threshold sends the same /b/ output for every token below its boundary. What does it predict for downstream effects of those tokens?
choices: No graded lexical difference attributable to the discarded variation
More competitor activation for every token nearer the boundary
A boundary shift produced by lexical feedback
Continuous downstream sensitivity despite identical transmitted symbols
why: If the output is identical, that output cannot carry graded uncertainty. A cascaded account preserves differences during transmission.

stem: A model continuously passes partial acoustic activation forward but has no backward connections. How should it be described?
choices: Cascaded without lexical feedback
Thresholded because the final response can be categorical
Feedback because information reaches more than one level
Cascaded only if words also influence phonemes
why: Cascading concerns continuous forward flow; feedback concerns reverse influence. They are logically separable properties.

stem: Which feature makes the furniture chain a thresholded-processing analogy?
choices: Each stage requires the preceding stage's completed output
Several levels use partially transformed material at the same time
Later stages revise earlier stages through reciprocal connections
A finished response hides earlier uncertainty from measurement
why: The waiting requirement is the point of the analogy. A cascade instead transmits changing partial states during processing.

stem: A drought immediately alters connected levels of a food web while populations keep changing. Which property does this illustrate?
choices: Ongoing propagation through interacting levels
Each level waits for another level's completed product
Only the final state can influence the next level
Reverse connections alone establish graded forward transmission
why: The analogy emphasizes continuous influence. Reciprocal influences add feedback, while a final response alone does not reveal this dynamics.

stem: Why track eyes while participants click bear or pear?
choices: Looks can reveal a competitor that loses the final choice
To establish the final label without measuring its time course
To remove lexical competition by presenting visual objects
To infer that every briefly viewed object was selected
why: Eye movements expose the developing competition. The endpoint can remain categorical even when earlier states are graded.

stem: McMurray finds step-like final identification and graded competitor looks. Which conclusion accommodates both?
choices: Categorical responses can emerge from graded processing
The categorical click proves a completed phoneme gate
Graded looks mean no categorical identification occurred
The eye movements measure only response errors after selection
why: The measures describe different stages of behavior. Graded internal competition can precede a stable final category response.

stem: Two tokens are both clicked as bear. The token nearer the boundary produces more looks to pear. What differs?
choices: The strength of temporary lexical competition
The categorical label assigned to the token
The word's dictionary meaning
The number of possible lexical candidates in the display
why: The final response is held constant; competitor looking differs. This isolates graded competition among tokens within one response category.

stem: Under cascading, what should happen to competitor looks as a token approaches its category boundary from within a category?
choices: They should increase gradually despite an unchanged final label
A constant competitor level until a phoneme threshold switches
Competitor activity determined only by the final click
Greater competitor activation only after the listener chooses it
why: Graded acoustic uncertainty continues influencing later levels. A sharp gate predicts less within-category differentiation downstream.

stem: A near-boundary bilabial stop partially supports /b/ and /p/. How can pear attract looks before a bear click?
choices: Partial feature evidence activates multiple phonemes and words
A discrete /b/ signal is identical across tokens, so lexical uncertainty is added later independently
The eye trace measures a second final answer rather than partial activation
The competitor activates only because its picture is visually similar
why: A cascade permits competing activation without two final selections. The stimulus does not have to literally contain two words.

stem: Beace facilitates war and ging facilitates queen. What explains the relevance of these nonword primes?
choices: Incomplete input partially activates real-word meanings
The nonword must first be accepted as a complete dictionary entry
The prime's resemblance influences responses without activating a related word
Priming arises only from a shared initial phoneme with the target
why: Near-word forms can activate peace or king enough to influence related targets. Perfect lexical input is not required for all downstream effects.

stem: Why does categorical labeling not establish a thresholded phoneme-to-word architecture?
choices: The response can be discrete while earlier activation remains graded
Final categorization directly specifies how every earlier stage transmitted information
All word recognition must be thresholded because it ends in one choice
A labeling task can measure lexical feedback without changing lexical context
why: The architecture concerns information flow, whereas labeling measures the response. McMurray's within-category effects distinguish those claims.

stem: Which connection counts specifically as lexical feedback?
choices: An activated word strengthens its component phoneme candidates
A feature continuously activates a compatible phoneme
A partially active phoneme activates several words
Competing words inhibit each other at the same lexical level
why: Feedback runs from a later lexical representation to an earlier phoneme level. The other activation examples are forward influences.

stem: Why compare word/nonword continua that favor opposite phoneme interpretations?
choices: Lexical context can be varied around similar acoustic ambiguity
To compare familiar and unfamiliar talkers' articulation
To ensure that the same response label always creates a word
To vary word frequency while removing phoneme ambiguity
why: Changing the surrounding sequence changes which label forms a word. This tests lexical influence on an ambiguous consonant.

stem: A student says Ganong merely found more word responses and ignores where the curves differ. What evidence is missed?
choices: The effect's concentration near the phoneme boundary
Whether endpoint tokens are ever correctly labeled
Whether participants are able to perform any labeling task
Whether all responses are shifted equally across the continuum
why: The distribution of the lexical effect across ambiguity distinguishes a boundary shift from a simpler uniform report adjustment.

stem: A lexical boundary-shift account predicts the largest effect for which tokens?
choices: Ambiguous tokens near the category transition
Clear endpoints because word knowledge is needed most when sound is certain
All continuum positions equally because the bias concerns reporting a word
Only the nonword endpoint because no acoustic evidence is used
why: Lexical information is most useful where acoustic evidence leaves uncertainty. Clear endpoints need less resolution by word knowledge.

stem: Ganong's curves differ mainly around the transition region. Which account does the lecture develop from this pattern?
choices: Word knowledge can alter ambiguous phoneme categorization
A uniform response correction unrelated to ambiguity
Identical labeling functions regardless of lexical context
Complete elimination of category distinctions by word knowledge
why: The boundary-related pattern motivates interactive lexical influence. It concerns perceived identity, not an acoustic change caused by spelling.

stem: In TRACE, the ending /g/ strongly favors plug over blood and blush. How can it affect the ambiguous onset?
choices: Plug activation feeds back to compatible phonemes
Final /g/ resolves only the current sound with no effect on lexical candidates
Initial phoneme identity must have been fully settled before any word activated
Word activation changes, but lexical-to-phoneme influence is excluded
why: Later evidence changes lexical competition; reciprocal connections then reinforce the favored word's phonemes, including the earlier ambiguous position.

stem: What important demand distinguishes TRACE's speech input from a static written-word display?
choices: Speech evidence unfolds and updates candidate support over time
Feedback is possible only in speech, not written-word models
The acoustic input becomes available all at once
Only written words can activate competing lexical representations
why: The models share interaction principles, but successive acoustic evidence makes temporal updating central to the speech simulation.

stem: An onset competitor attracts early looks and then declines as the target ending arrives. What does the cohort effect demonstrate?
choices: Lexical candidates compete before the entire word is resolved
Lexical processing begins only after a complete word is delivered
An onset competitor must share the target's meaning
A competitor's brief activation necessarily changes the final response
why: The rise and decline trace changing compatibility with the unfolding sound. Correct recognition can include temporary competitor activation.

stem: A patient understands a heard word but struggles with verbatim repetition. Why did disconnection models find such a pattern informative?
choices: Comprehension and repetition can depend on different connections
Comprehension and repetition are one operation with different names
A repetition error identifies a loss of every lexical meaning
Fluency alone determines whether the heard word was understood
why: Different routes can support meaning access and repetition. A selective failure motivates a specified connection rather than loss of every language operation.

stem: Fluent speech contains neologisms and substitutions, while comprehension is poor. Which distinction prevents equating fluent with normal language?
choices: Speech flow and meaningful lexical organization are different dimensions
Fluent articulation establishes intact comprehension despite substitutions
Neologisms are direct evidence of an isolated motor-planning deficit
Syntactically shaped output guarantees intact lexical selection
why: Wernicke-type fluency can coexist with lexical and comprehension disruption. Fluent output alone does not establish accurate language processing.

stem: A patient omits grammatical particles but preserves major content words. What does telegraphic describe?
choices: The reduced organization of the speech output
The underlying grammatical system independently of task demands
A uniquely localized lesion defined only by its anatomical name
The speed of articulation without reference to grammatical form
why: Telegraphic describes behavior. Additional tasks are needed to determine whether knowledge, processing resources, or motor constraints explain it.

stem: Why is it misleading to treat Broca's original patients as perfect examples of every later definition of Broca's aphasia?
choices: Profound speech-motor difficulty is not identical to agrammatic grammar impairment
A fluent comprehension disorder is the defining historical observation
The later syndrome concerns only articulation and never comprehension
All agrammatic output directly identifies the original motor deficit
why: The lecture distinguishes apraxia-like articulate-speech problems from later grammar-centered syndrome interpretations.

stem: Why do lemma selection and positional organization matter to the grammar–lexicon proposal?
choices: They distinguish selecting lexical representations from arranging grammatical forms
They equate choosing a lemma with arranging its affixes
They imply grammatical assembly is unnecessary once meanings are selected
They identify lexical meanings solely through speech-movement timing
why: The levels offer candidate operations behind different deficits. Morphological assembly illustrates why lexical meaning and structural organization should not be conflated.

stem: Why examine comprehension when a patient produces agrammatic speech with motor difficulty?
choices: It tests language relations without requiring fluent articulation
It removes all memory and attention demands from the task
It establishes competence directly regardless of the chosen sentences
It tests only whether the patient can recognize the nouns
why: Comprehension can reduce production demands, though it still involves performance. It helps test whether the difficulty extends beyond speech movements.

stem: A patient correctly pictures the dog bit the man. Why is that insufficient to show intact syntax?
choices: Plausibility and familiar word order can provide compensating cues
Only sentence length can determine successful comprehension
The sentence is ungrammatical and cannot test interpretation
A correct picture choice necessarily uses every syntactic relation
why: Several cues converge on a dog-bites-man event. A diagnostic contrast makes structure disagree with an easy meaning-based shortcut.

stem: In the dog that the man is biting is angry, which interpretation requires the structural relationships?
choices: The man bites the dog, and the dog is angry
The dog bites the man, and the dog is angry
The man bites the dog, and the man is angry
The dog and man exchange grammatical roles at the main verb
why: The embedded subject man performs biting; dog is its object and the main-clause subject. A plausibility shortcut can reverse those roles.

stem: Why include reversible and improbable center-embedded sentences alongside semantically constrained ones?
choices: To vary whether world knowledge can compensate for structural difficulty
To measure lexical familiarity while holding event plausibility irrelevant
To ensure every embedded sentence can be solved by likely event knowledge
To infer grammar from speech production without a comprehension response
why: Reversible items allow role exchange; improbable items oppose expectations. Comparing them with constrained items tests the contribution of syntactic role assignment.

stem: Broca-type patients struggle especially when syntax conflicts with likely roles; Wernicke-type patients are poor more broadly. What motivated the original inference?
choices: A relatively specific structural-comprehension difficulty in Broca's group
Broca's patients showed fully intact comprehension across conditions
The two patient groups differed only in articulation rate
The comparison directly ruled out general processing demands
why: The contrast motivated a syntax account, but broader task comparisons are needed to test language specificity.

stem: Why replace a broad label such as poor comprehension with controlled task contrasts?
choices: Different operations can produce the same broad symptom
Specific task contrasts eliminate all individual variability
A syndrome name independently establishes a single underlying mechanism
Broad symptom totals identify structural computation more directly than contrasts
why: Specific contrasts isolate candidate operations, allowing a more precise structure–function question than an overall behavioral label.

stem: In it's the cat that the dog is biting, participants must identify the actor. Which response follows syntax rather than first-noun order?
choices: Dog
Cat, because the first noun is always the agent
Both, because a cleft assigns equal actor roles
Cat, because the embedded object becomes the main-clause agent
why: The object cleft places cat first but dog remains the agent. Naming order and action role are separated by the structure.

stem: Object clefts and passives cause greater difficulty than active forms in patient groups. What must a successful explanation address?
choices: The extra cost of noncanonical role assignment as well as overall accuracy
Only the overall difference between patients and controls
The number of nouns correctly recognized without assigning roles
The first-mentioned animal independently of grammatical form
why: The relevant pattern includes both general impairment and selective sentence-form costs. Neither vocabulary naming nor a single total score captures both.

stem: Healthy undergraduates under speed or memory demands show similar vulnerability to complex sentence forms. Which explanation gains support?
choices: Processing-resource limits can generate a structurally selective pattern
The sentence-specific pattern uniquely proves loss of grammar
Speed stress changes the sentence's grammatical structure
Healthy listeners' mistakes cannot inform patient processing accounts
why: The manipulation produces performance stress without the clinical lesion. Similar profiles make a resource-based contribution plausible.

stem: Saygin compares verbal and nonverbal action–object matching. Why retain the action relation while changing its presentation?
choices: To test whether difficulty extends beyond linguistic input
To replace an interpretation task with a pure articulation task
To determine whether visual input can repair every linguistic deficit
To hold language constant while changing the action relation
why: Preserving the relevant relation tests language specificity. Difficulty across formats suggests a broader contribution than sentence grammar alone.

stem: Nonverbal action matching correlates with damage involving Broca's area. What interpretation fits best?
choices: The region's contribution may extend to operations shared with nonverbal action tasks
Any association with Broca's area must be syntactic by definition
A nonverbal task measures only visual acuity rather than event relations
The anatomical result proves that the clinical group has no language difficulty
why: A lesion association outside verbal stimuli challenges exclusivity, without making the region irrelevant to language tasks.

stem: A patient has trouble matching both words and meaningful environmental sounds to pictures. Which shared demand deserves consideration?
choices: Connecting auditory patterns with meanings
Selecting the correct grammatical suffix for an action
Mapping the first noun onto an agent without sound interpretation
Planning the articulatory form of a pictured object's name
why: Both tasks involve auditory meaning access. Their similarity tests whether poor verbal comprehension reflects a broader auditory processing contribution.

stem: Both verbal and nonverbal sound-matching deficits associate with posterior language-region damage. Why combine behavioral and lesion evidence?
choices: They connect a cross-format deficit with overlapping anatomical associations
Imaging establishes the task's computation independently of behavioral design
The overlap proves verbal and nonverbal representations are identical
A posterior association uniquely identifies word-specific representations
why: The measures converge on a broader auditory-comprehension contribution. Task details still define what the anatomical association explains.

stem: Which research strategy most clearly advances the grammar-specific versus general-processing debate?
choices: Compare matched linguistic and nonlinguistic demands quantitatively
Classify each patient by syndrome before considering the task pattern
Use a single fluent-speech score as the measure of grammar
Infer a missing computation from the clinical label alone
why: Matched contrasts turn competing explanations into measurable predictions. A syndrome label alone does not isolate the operation causing difficulty.

stem: Voxel-based mapping finds anterior associations with broad fluency deficits and posterior associations with broad comprehension deficits. What claim matches its level of measurement?
choices: A rough production–perception dissociation for those symptom measures
A complete grammar–lexicon dissociation independent of task definition
A one-to-one map between every syndrome and named region
Proof that posterior tissue processes only words and no other sounds
why: Broad symptoms support a broad anatomical relationship. More specific computational claims require more specifically designed behavioral contrasts.

stem: Why does generativity challenge a stored-list account of acquisition?
choices: Children can understand and produce sentences never previously encountered
Children retain frequent complete sentences more accurately than rare ones
Children recognize some sounds before naming objects
Vocabulary contains arbitrary links between sounds and referents
why: Generativity requires explaining productive combinations, not just memory for specific complete utterances.

stem: Which finding would most directly undermine the claim that grammatical reinforcement alone teaches grammar?
choices: Reliable grammar develops without consistent reward for grammaticality
Children receive encouragement when a message is communicatively successful
Grammatical and ungrammatical utterances differ in surface frequency
Children repeat a form after an adult has just used it
why: The critique targets the mismatch between required reward contingencies and actual acquisition conditions, not the mere existence of repetition.

stem: Why was categorical perception initially attractive as evidence for a language-specific mechanism?
choices: Perceived similarity appeared organized by linguistic categories
Identification tasks always require a small set of response categories
Formant differences can be manipulated without changing lexical context
Listeners can recognize the same message from variable speakers
why: The early interpretation linked acoustic grouping to symbolic speech categories. Later cross-domain evidence tests its claimed exclusivity.

stem: In an infant habituation experiment, what comparison best isolates discrimination rather than a general rise in responding?
choices: Recovery after a sound change compared with an unchanged condition
A high sucking rate without a comparable unchanged condition
Recovery measured only before a new token is presented
A final word choice without measuring the infant's behavioral change
why: A no-change condition helps distinguish detection of the manipulation from general response variation.

stem: Why match the physical size of within- and between-category VOT changes?
choices: To ask whether category relationship predicts recovery beyond acoustic distance
To assume that within-category tokens are physically identical
To ensure the two conditions have equal perceived differences
To make a labeling task unnecessary for defining every adult boundary
why: A matched change can have different perceptual effects depending on the category boundary. This is the critical categorical comparison.

stem: Why did Eimas's infant result motivate nativist interest without by itself proving language specificity?
choices: The behavior appears early, but early behaviors can use broader perceptual capacities
The infants' sucking response measures the complete grammar directly
Early appearance implies that no experience could have affected the behavior
The method directly separates innate auditory capacity from every learned influence
why: Early appearance concerns developmental timing. Nonspeech and animal comparisons address different claims about the mechanism.

stem: Younger English-learning infants discriminate a nonnative contrast better than older English-learning infants. What additional comparison most helps identify language tuning?
choices: Age-matched infants whose language preserves the contrast
Older English-learning infants tested only on the native contrast
Younger English-learning infants tested only on an easier contrast
Adult English readers' explicit knowledge of the contrast names
why: Relevant language experience can preserve sensitivity, separating selective tuning from a uniform developmental loss.

stem: A pure selection-from-universal-contrasts account predicts what initial state?
choices: The relevant contrasts are available before language-specific narrowing
All contrasts require native-language exposure to become initially detectable
The native categories emerge only after word meanings are acquired
Every early category boundary remains unchanged by experience
why: The narrative treats experience as selecting among initially available distinctions. Experience-dependent emergence tests that premise.

stem: Which combination most directly challenges both speech exclusivity and human exclusivity of categorical perception?
choices: Nonspeech categorization and chinchilla speech categorization
Early infant speech discrimination and adult speech labeling alone
Two native-language contrasts with different acoustic distances
A native speaker's vocabulary size and sentence-production speed
why: Nonspeech findings address the stimulus domain; nonhuman findings address the species restriction. They test distinct aspects of specialization.

stem: Adults discriminate equal nonspeech differences best across a pluck–bow boundary. Which inference is justified?
choices: Category-linked discrimination can arise beyond language
The nonspeech sounds are implicitly treated as linguistic units
Any sharp labeling function alone identifies the perceptual mechanism
Category-linked discrimination must disappear without meaningful words
why: The perceptual signature extends beyond speech. It does not turn the stimuli into linguistic units.

stem: Infant sucking recovers for between-category nonspeech changes but not matched within-category changes. What explains the comparison?
choices: Early categorical organization is not restricted to speech input
The within-category condition contains no acoustic shift
Infants recover because they recognize a new word
The result identifies a uniquely phonemic form of habituation
why: The physical manipulation occurs in both change conditions; the different behavioral response follows the perceptual grouping.

stem: In the chinchilla training, what does an SD signal?
choices: That a response can receive its trained reward
That the animal has formed a complete human phoneme inventory
That every intermediate stimulus will receive the same response
That successful responding necessarily involves lexical meaning
why: A discriminative stimulus controls rewarded responding. Endpoint training can reveal categorization without human lexical understanding.

stem: Young infants detect /ma/–/na/ but not /na/–/ŋa/ comparably. Which claim is weakened?
choices: Every speech contrast is equally salient at the outset
Initial speech perception is already narrowed to one adult language
All speech contrasts depend on conscious explicit instruction
The easier contrast must have larger syllable meanings
why: Unequal initial salience contradicts a fully uniform starting inventory, without denying perception or later learning.

stem: Filipino-learning infants improve on the difficult nasal contrast with age. What process must be added to simple loss-only narrowing?
choices: Experience-dependent strengthening or acquisition of a distinction
Selective retention of two initially equally discriminable categories
A general improvement independent of the language environment
The appearance of vocabulary without a change in perception
why: The direction of change is improvement. Learning can organize a distinction that was not initially behaviorally clear.

stem: In the associative illustration, why can a bell eventually influence salivation?
choices: Experience strengthens a connection when relevant activity co-occurs
The bell first becomes a symbolic word for food
Food and bell connections strengthen equally without co-occurrence
Reward eliminates the need for any representation of the stimulus
why: Associative change depends on patterned co-activation. The example supplies a learning mechanism to extend toward more complex recognition.

stem: What does a statistical vowel learner extract from a cloud in F1–F2 space?
choices: Where productions cluster and how their values are distributed
One exact acoustic point defining every possible vowel token
A prototype supplied entirely by an adult verbal label
The total token frequency without their acoustic distribution
why: A distribution can support a prototype or category despite variation and overlap among individual productions.

stem: In Maye's study, test tokens 3 and 6 occurred equally often during exposure in both groups. Why is that important?
choices: Different test responses can be linked to overall distribution shape
It guarantees identical category learning in both conditions
It makes the two overall distributions equivalent
It rules out any contribution of surrounding input structure
why: Equal exposure to the critical tokens limits a simple token-familiarity explanation while unimodal versus bimodal context differs.

stem: After bimodal versus unimodal exposure, only one group distinguishes alternating from repeated test tokens. Which pattern fits distributional learning?
choices: Bimodal exposure supports treating the two tokens as different categories
Unimodal exposure supports greater separation of the test tokens
Both groups must label the tokens explicitly as different phonemes
The critical difference is simply how often tokens 3 and 6 occurred
why: Two peaks support a two-category organization. The task measures sensitivity to the token distinction, not vocabulary.

stem: Live Mandarin exposure supports learning more clearly than audio or television exposure. What factor does this comparison highlight?
choices: Social and interactive conditions of exposure
Only the number of Mandarin words infants can already produce
A purely acoustic exposure count independent of interaction
The necessity of television-specific visual cues for category learning
why: The contrast concerns how input is encountered. The lecture develops social reinforcement and guided learning as candidate explanations.

stem: Which statement best represents constrained statistical learning?
choices: Learning depends on relevant features, prior organization, and social context
A learner extracts every varying property with equal readiness
Social interaction is a reward added after statistical learning is complete
Earlier categories affect final responses but never subsequent learning
why: Constraints determine what regularities are tracked and how effectively they change the learner. They are not a denial of statistical sensitivity.

stem: Why is segmenting speech not equivalent to splitting at silence?
choices: Pauses and closures do not consistently coincide with word boundaries
Every closure consistently marks the beginning of a new word
Pauses locate syllable boundaries and thereby uniquely locate all words
Knowing the acoustic waveform automatically supplies the segmentation
why: Segmentation requires discovering recurring linguistic units despite a continuous signal with unreliable silence markers.

stem: Infants recognize kingdom in passages more readily than device after familiarization. What cue is implicated?
choices: English's frequent initial-stress pattern
A language-independent preference for the longest familiarized word
A guarantee that every English word has initial stress
Explicit knowledge of the two words' meanings
why: Kingdom has initial stress; device does not. The result links segmentation to a useful but language-dependent stress cue.

stem: An unlikely within-word sound sequence appears in connected speech. How can phonotactic knowledge help?
choices: It can favor a boundary between the sounds
It uniquely determines the intended meaning of each segment
It supplies the same boundary cues in every language
It makes stress irrelevant once one sound pair is recognized
why: Phonotactics constrains likely within-word combinations, providing evidence about boundaries without uniquely determining meaning.

stem: Why compare the frequency of a syllable pair with the frequency of its starting syllable?
choices: The ratio expresses how predictable the continuation is given the start
The count of the pair alone measures its conditional predictability
The denominator should contain only successful pair repetitions
The ratio measures whether the two syllables share a meaning
why: Transitional probability concerns a conditional relationship, not the raw pair count alone.

stem: Ice cream and I scream illustrate what point about segmentation cues?
choices: The same acoustic sequence can support competing divisions
Speech statistics cannot ever support word segmentation
Every acoustic sequence has one invariant boundary structure
Stress alone always resolves competing divisions correctly
why: Segmentation uses probabilistic cues and context. Ambiguous divisions do not make statistical information irrelevant.

stem: Why use monotone, continuous CV-syllable streams in Saffran's experiment?
choices: To reduce prosodic, phonotactic, and pause cues to trained boundaries
To make each word recognizable through isolated presentation
To emphasize stress as the only remaining boundary cue
To test whether familiar meanings improve statistical learning
why: Removing alternative boundary cues isolates the informational role of transition statistics.

stem: The artificial stream has no spaces, yet internal syllables reliably predict each other. What can a statistical learner recover?
choices: Recurring units from predictable internal transitions
The meanings of the units from conditional probability alone
A unique grouping supplied by physical pauses
An explicit rule that an adult had to teach verbally
why: The structure is present in conditional relationships even when explicit boundary markers and meanings are absent.

stem: A colored printout reveals the artificial words. Why should the colors not be treated as an infant cue?
choices: The colors visualize groupings that were not supplied in the auditory stimulus
The colors changed how frequently each auditory unit occurred
The infant received the same colored word labels as the experimenter
The visualization demonstrates that the sound had audible boundaries
why: The experimenter-facing visualization and the participant's actual input differ. Learning must be explained from what the infant heard.

stem: A trained word and a boundary-spanning part-word occur equally often. Why compare them?
choices: It separates transition structure from simple sequence-frequency familiarity
It ensures equal conditional predictability inside both sequences
It compares familiar words with sequences never heard at all
It removes differences in segmentation while testing only referent learning
why: Equal raw frequency can coexist with different internal predictability. That difference tests statistical segmentation more specifically.

stem: GOPILA and BU-GIKO both occur twice, but GI follows BU on only some BU occasions. What differs?
choices: The probability of the continuation given its preceding syllable
Only the complete strings' raw frequencies
Only the experimental test duration
The probability of the whole stream independent of the starting syllable
why: The conditional denominator includes all starting-syllable occurrences. Equal full-string counts do not guarantee equal transitional probabilities.

stem: Infants prefer part-words over frequency-matched trained words at test. What does the novelty effect support?
choices: Sensitivity to learned sequence structure beyond raw frequency
Part-words were more familiar because longer looking always indicates familiarity
Part-words were unfamiliar solely because they never occurred during exposure
The response establishes knowledge of what the artificial words mean
why: The task's novelty interpretation follows its exposure design. Distinguishing matched-frequency strings supports learning their statistical organization.

stem: Why does hearing cat near an animal not uniquely determine its meaning?
choices: The word could refer to the whole, a part, a property, or an individual
The sound category alone specifies which part of the scene is named
The most visually salient feature must be the referent by definition
Recognizing a segmented form already establishes a whole-object meaning
why: The inductive problem concerns competing mappings in the same scene. Additional biases and social evidence narrow that hypothesis space.

stem: What does joint attention add beyond two people merely seeing an object?
choices: A shared communicative focus that supports reference
A requirement that the child and adult look at the same time without communication
Direct evidence that every gaze shift establishes a new word meaning
A default rule that only the object in the child's hand can be named
why: Sharing focus helps identify what a speaker intends to name. Mere simultaneous visibility does not provide the same interaction.

stem: An interacting adult's label is learned, but a behind-screen voice's label is not, despite the infant handling the object. What simple explanation is weakened?
choices: Temporal label–object co-occurrence alone is sufficient
Infants can never learn from recordings in any task
The spoken label was sufficient regardless of communicative setting
The infant's current attention alone uniquely established the intended referent
why: Both conditions pair a label with the handled object. Their difference highlights the communicative context beyond simple pairing.

stem: An adult looks into a bucket while naming a toy different from the infant's current toy. What distinguishes intention use from a self-focus association?
choices: Mapping the word toward the adult's intended object
Mapping to the child's held toy because it co-occurs with the label
Choosing the most visually familiar object regardless of gaze
Treating the adult's word as a label for the bucket itself
why: Discrepant labeling separates the speaker's focus from the infant's. Following intention can override the simple simultaneous-self-focus mapping.

stem: In Akhtar's task, an adult's expression helps infants identify a novel word's referent. What inference is involved?
choices: Using a goal or reaction to infer intended reference
Associating the label with whichever object was seen most recently
Mapping equally to every object that appeared during the search
Using only which object the infant handled at the moment of labeling
why: Affective and behavioral cues identify what the speaker means, extending reference learning beyond gaze alone.

stem: A new noun is used near an unfamiliar object with an unusual handle. What does the whole-object assumption initially favor?
choices: Naming the entire object
Naming the visually distinctive part before the whole
Selecting a property because it varies more than object identity
Interpreting every novel noun as an action performed with the object
why: The default narrows the candidate meaning toward the whole entity. It remains revisable with additional evidence.

stem: A familiar dog and an unfamiliar object are present when a new label is requested. Mutual exclusivity predicts which preference?
choices: The object without an already known name
The already named dog because familiar referents always take priority
Either object equally because known labels supply no information
The unfamiliar object's most salient property rather than the entity
why: The strategy uses existing names to favor an otherwise unnamed referent. It is a default, not a universal ban on multiple labels.

stem: Why is mommy up insufficient by itself to establish an adult-like productive construction?
choices: A formula, relevant-word list, or flexible pattern can yield a short utterance
The number of words uniquely determines the underlying construction
A formula must already have the same productive grammar as an adult pattern
Context is irrelevant once two different nouns have appeared
why: Context and generalization distinguish competing explanations of the same surface output.

stem: Children match the duck is gorping the bunny to a novel duck-on-bunny action. Why is a new verb useful?
choices: It tests use of transitive structure beyond memorized verb-specific phrases
It tests a familiar action name without structural generalization
It shows that production length and comprehension must coincide
It makes actor–recipient roles recoverable from the verb's known meaning
why: Word order can assign roles despite an unfamiliar verb, supporting generalization and comprehension beyond limited production.

stem: Adults improve after intensive training even though early learning is easier. Which timing account most naturally accommodates both?
choices: A sensitive period with later plasticity
A critical period in which the relevant learning is impossible afterward
An age-independent system with equal learning efficiency throughout life
An early window that remains open indefinitely whenever input is absent
why: Sensitive periods permit age-related advantages without requiring zero learning afterward.

stem: A corrected childhood cataract leaves poor vision in the affected eye. What explains the continuing deficit?
choices: Early abnormal input changed later cortical organization
The peripheral deficit must be unchanged despite treatment
The better eye prevents light from reaching the corrected eye
The outcome reflects only current input, not earlier organization
why: The peripheral problem can be repaired while its developmental cortical consequences persist.

stem: What does colonization by the better eye mean in the lecture's account?
choices: Its input gains a competitive cortical advantage
The stronger eye physically displaces the weaker eye's retinal tissue
The weaker eye has no initial cortical connections at all
The two eyes become identical inputs after the first exposure
why: The metaphor describes representation in a competitive system, not literal movement of an eye.

stem: Why patch the better eye rather than continually relying on it?
choices: Reducing its dominance lets the weaker eye drive learning
It repairs the weaker eye's optical defect directly
It improves vision by reducing input from both eyes equally
It prevents experience from changing the already formed cortical balance
why: Patching changes the balance of cortical use, allowing plasticity in the disadvantaged system.

stem: What does adult amblyopic perceptual learning show about an early optimal window?
choices: Later change can occur under suitably intensive experience
Early input history has no persistent effect once training begins
Ordinary adult exposure automatically restores normal vision
The early advantage was only a difference in peripheral anatomy
why: Adult improvement challenges a permanent complete loss of plasticity, while preserving an early advantage and developmental costs.

stem: Which sequence captures the amblyopia example?
choices: Early input imbalance, altered competition, persistent cost, possible training benefit
Current optical repair immediately restores the original cortical balance
The cortical outcome is independent of the initial deprivation
Treatment helps by reinforcing the stronger eye's existing advantage
why: The example links developmental history to lasting organization and experience-dependent rebalancing.

stem: Why distinguish accessible language from simply being exposed to speech sounds in a deaf child's history?
choices: The learner needs input that can actually support language acquisition
Sign can serve only as a second language after spoken language
Any ambient speech provides equivalent accessible linguistic input
Early access matters only for vocabulary and not structural knowledge
why: The deprivation question concerns access to a usable language. Sign languages provide linguistic input through another modality.

stem: What motivated Lenneberg's maturational proposal?
choices: Connecting stage-like language development with neurological change
A direct observation of one neural switch at a fixed closing age
Evidence that stages are learned only through explicit reward
Identical recovery after the same injury in children and adults
why: The synthesis linked language milestones and brain development. It did not establish an absolute inability to learn any linguistic information later.

stem: Why does a large age gap in postmortem brain measurements matter?
choices: It limits the precision of a proposed developmental timeline
It confirms that no developmental changes occurred in the missing ages
It independently establishes the exact onset and offset of the window
It makes a sparse neurological description a controlled acquisition experiment
why: Sparse measurements can motivate a hypothesis but cannot provide a continuously observed timetable.

stem: Why were childhood hemispherectomy outcomes relevant to cerebral-dominance accounts?
choices: They suggested more flexible early organization than comparable adult outcomes
They demonstrated equivalent outcomes after early and adult injury
They proved the remaining hemisphere always restores every skill completely
They directly measured the quality of all childhood language input
why: The contrast concerns developmental reorganization after injury. It motivated a link to changing lateralization.

stem: Children with perinatal stroke do better than comparable adults but may remain low-normal. Which conclusion respects both observations?
choices: Early resilience can coexist with persistent language costs
Better outcomes establish complete recovery to the same trajectory
Low-normal outcomes show no early advantage over adulthood
The outcome is explained only by the side of injury, irrespective of age
why: Relative improvement and full normalization are different claims. The outcome pattern supports substantial but incomplete compensation.

stem: Why examine vocabulary and grammar separately in Genie rather than give one learned-language score?
choices: They developed unevenly after delayed experience
Vocabulary is a direct substitute measure for all grammatical knowledge
A single age score would already identify which component changed
Comprehension and production necessarily reflect identical demands
why: The component contrast is central to the timing argument and would be hidden by one undifferentiated score.

stem: Genie learned many words and some plural comprehension. What does this rule out?
choices: A complete inability to learn any language-related information later
A persistent disadvantage for grammar relative to vocabulary
A role for early experience in later outcomes
A difference between comprehension and production development
why: Substantial later learning is compatible with selective or persistent difficulties. It contradicts only the strongest all-learning-is-impossible claim.

stem: Why should Genie's production deficit not be read simply as the size of her vocabulary knowledge?
choices: Comprehension, grammar, and speaking demands differed, including her history of punishment
Her spoken output uniquely measures everything she understands
Vocabulary size and grammatical production must develop at equal rates
Punishment of vocalization rules out any later comprehension learning
why: Output reflects several demands and experiences. Her comprehension–production gap requires a component-based explanation.

stem: What pattern specifically motivated an L1 grammar-timing interpretation in Genie?
choices: Vocabulary developed more readily than grammar
Complete absence of later vocabulary learning
A controlled age manipulation with all other experience matched
Preservation of a fully acquired first language from early childhood
why: The relative learning pattern was suggestive, while the unusual deprivation history complicates causal attribution.

stem: Two groups start ASL late; one had an early spoken L1 and the other had no accessible early language. Why is that contrast important?
choices: It separates late learning of a language from late access to any language
It equates both the onset of ASL and the onset of any language
It isolates language modality while holding all prior linguistic experience constant
It compares two groups whose early language foundations are identical
why: Comparable later sign onset can coexist with different foundations. Prior language experience changes the interpretation of age at ASL acquisition.

stem: Late L2 sign learners outperform late L1 sign learners. Which explanation is supported?
choices: An established early language foundation benefits later language learning
Age at learning ASL alone determines performance regardless of early access
Spoken input is required because sign cannot establish a first language
Late L1 and late L2 impose the same learning problem by definition
why: The contrast points to early accessible language experience, not a requirement for speech specifically.

stem: If withholding L1 does not preserve child-like later acquisition, which simple idea is weakened?
choices: The learning window stays open indefinitely until first use
Maturation can affect learning even without normal input
Early accessible language contributes to later learning
Vocabulary and grammar can show different learning outcomes
why: Deprivation does not simply pause development. The timing history continues to matter before first accessible language arrives.

stem: Which claim best matches the lecture's first-language evidence?
choices: Early accessible experience is important, with different later learning and recovery possibilities
Every later learning success rules out any sensitive-period effect
All components share one exact cutoff regardless of experience
A rare case is equivalent to experimentally randomized deprivation
why: The evidence converges on early experience while differing in histories and measured components. It does not establish a universal all-or-none cutoff.

stem: How does adult visual learning sharpen a language critical-period discussion?
choices: It distinguishes an early advantage from complete abolition of plasticity
It establishes identical neural representations for vision and grammar
It directly determines the treatment needed for every late L1 learner
It shows later learning has the same efficiency as early acquisition
why: The visual example supplies a conceptual distinction about timing. It is an analogy, not direct evidence of identical language mechanisms.

stem: In the horse raced past the barn fell, what is the successful structural interpretation?
choices: The horse that was raced past the barn subsequently fell
The horse raced and then fell, with raced as the sole main verb throughout
The barn is the understood subject of fell
Raced and fell jointly form one unchanged main predicate without a modifier
why: Raced begins a reduced relative modifying horse; fell is the main predicate. That interpretation requires revising the initially attractive main-verb reading.

stem: Why does a garden path support incremental processing?
choices: Later words force revision of an interpretation already underway
Difficulty appears only after a completed sentence has been assigned no structure
All structurally ambiguous sentences lack a grammatical interpretation
A single correct endpoint reveals the absence of earlier commitment
why: Reanalysis costs indicate an earlier commitment. Difficulty alone does not mean the sentence lacks a grammatical analysis.

stem: A minimal-attachment parser encounters a locally ambiguous reduced relative. Which initial preference follows?
choices: The analysis requiring fewer structural nodes
The analysis most consistent with world knowledge before any structural choice
Every possible analysis maintained equally until the final word
The analysis containing the richest set of embedded relations
why: Minimal attachment is a structural economy preference. Later information can require abandoning its initially simpler analysis.

stem: In the burglar blew open the safe with the dynamite, the preferred action attachment makes dynamite what?
choices: The instrument of blowing open the safe
A property identifying which safe was opened
The subject performing the opening action
A modifier of the burglar's identity rather than the action
why: Attaching with the dynamite to the action specifies its instrument; noun attachment instead describes the safe.

stem: Why is with the jewels harder in the corresponding safe sentence?
choices: The plausible noun attachment conflicts with the preferred action attachment
The noun attachment is ungrammatical but semantically attractive
Jewels is simply less familiar, independent of attachment
The structural preference automatically changes before meaning is evaluated
why: The reader may first treat jewels as an instrument, then reattach the phrase to the safe to obtain the sensible relation.

stem: Which observation is most awkward for a strictly syntax-first account of the initial parse?
choices: The same sentence's early interpretation changes with referential context
Meaning corrects a structural analysis only after a mismatch
A parser favors economical trees in an ambiguous sentence
A later word sometimes requires reanalysis
why: Early contextual influence challenges autonomy of the initial choice. Later correction is already compatible with a syntax-first sequence.

stem: Many reduced relatives are easy when meaning and usage favor them. What conclusion does the constraint-based account draw?
choices: Difficulty depends on interacting structural, lexical, and semantic support
Reduced relatives are intrinsically difficult regardless of lexical content
Semantics matters only after an independent parser completes its task
Only the number of structural nodes determines reading cost
why: The same construction can have different competition depending on its words and context.

stem: Why may the burglar arrested in the parking lot be easier than the corresponding policeman sentence?
choices: Burglar favors the undergoer role, supporting the reduced relative
Burglar is more likely than policeman to perform an arrest
The two nouns favor exactly the same agent expectations
The difference eliminates reduced-relative structure from the first sentence
why: World knowledge favors a burglar being arrested. A policeman more strongly supports the competing agent interpretation.

stem: In the one-apple task, why are looks to the empty towel informative?
choices: They indicate a temporary destination interpretation
They establish that the empty towel was the final required destination
They measure knowledge of towel without interpreting the instruction
They show the listener had already resolved the full instruction correctly
why: The final instruction targets the box. Attraction to the wrong destination reveals the competing analysis during the instruction.

stem: Adding a second apple makes on the towel useful for identifying the target. What eye pattern follows the lecture?
choices: Fewer looks to the empty towel as a destination
More looks to the empty towel because two apples increase every ambiguity equally
Identical early looks because context can act only after syntactic completion
An inability to select either apple despite the identifying phrase
why: The phrase now serves referential identification early, reducing competition from the destination analysis.

stem: What is held constant in the one- versus two-apple comparison that makes the contextual effect important?
choices: The spoken ambiguous instruction
The number of apples and their locations
The need to distinguish one referent from another
All contextual information supplied by the scene
why: The same sentence changes its early interpretation with the scene. Referential context is the critical manipulated source of support.

stem: A mouse trajectory curves toward an incorrect destination before reaching the correct one. What does the trajectory add to endpoint accuracy?
choices: Evidence of competition during the unfolding action
It directly identifies one stored syntactic tree
It proves the incorrect destination was ultimately selected
It measures only the completed response with greater spatial precision
why: Movement can preserve intermediate attraction that a correct final endpoint hides, much like eye movements.

stem: What does time-locking an ERP to a word allow researchers to assess?
choices: When a contextual manipulation changes the measured response
Which single linguistic module must generate the entire response
Whether grammar knowledge is present independently of task design
Only whether the participant eventually notices an error
why: Temporal alignment tests response timing. Identifying its mechanism still requires appropriately contrasted stimuli.

stem: Why is eaten disruptive in the pizza was in the eaten?
choices: Its category conflicts with the noun-phrase continuation set up by in the
The word cannot be recognized because it is not in the lexicon
It is semantically odd but structurally expected after the determiner
The context supplies no category expectation before eaten appears
why: Familiar words can violate the required grammatical position. Recognition of the word and structural fit are distinct.

stem: What does the early timing of an ELAN establish most directly?
choices: A rapid response difference to the manipulated word-category context
A demonstrated grammar-only computation independent of perceptual cues
Proof that semantic and visual predictions cannot operate rapidly
A universal response to every unexpected word regardless of form
why: Timing constrains the process but does not alone determine its computation. Form-based contrasts test the source of the early effect.

stem: How can a syntactic expectation affect early visual processing?
choices: Expected categories activate predictions about associated word forms
The expected grammatical category changes the printed letters themselves
Syntactic effects must wait for all visual processing to finish
Only explicit grammatical rules can generate visual expectations
why: Learned relations between form and category let higher-level context predict visual patterns. Mismatches can then appear early.

stem: Perches is a noun in one sentence and a verb in another. Why is that useful experimentally?
choices: Form identity can be separated from the category required by context
Contextual category is fixed because the written form stays identical
The manipulation isolates meaning while holding grammatical role unchanged
A form's typical category completely determines its role in every sentence
why: An ambiguous form allows contextual role and typical form associations to be distinguished rather than conflated.

stem: Perches is relatively noun-like in form but used as a verb. Which question follows from form-prediction accounts?
choices: Whether typical form and contextual category jointly affect early responses
Whether typical form fixes grammatical role regardless of context
Whether the same spelling can ever occur in two categories
Whether statistical form information is available only after sentence completion
why: Form typicality and required category supply potentially conflicting evidence. Their interaction is the target of the comparison.

stem: An early effect appears for strongly noun-like violations but not neutral nouns. Which account is supported?
choices: Early category effects depend partly on physically available form cues
A category effect must occur equally for every noun once its role is known
Neutral nouns cannot be integrated syntactically at all
The early effect establishes an exclusively abstract syntactic computation
why: The contrast links the early response to morphology or statistical form typicality rather than category labels alone.

stem: Which pairing correctly links a sentence to its main lesson?
choices: Apple-on-towel: referential context can shape early parsing
Horse-raced: a grammatical sentence cannot create a processing cost
Colorless-green: sensible meaning is necessary for grammatical structure
Bird-perches: early word-category effects are independent of form statistics
why: The apple manipulation holds the string constant while changing referential context. The other pairings reverse the lecture's conclusions.

stem: An adult learns initial L2 vocabulary quickly but does not reach native-like proficiency later. Why is this not contradictory?
choices: Initial learning rate and ultimate attainment are different outcomes
Ultimate attainment is the number of words acquired in the first lesson
Adults' initial advantage guarantees native-like eventual performance
Children must outperform adults at every phase for an age effect to exist
why: The lecture distinguishes early speed from eventual proficiency. Transfer and general skills can help initial learning without ensuring a native-like endpoint.

stem: Why can older L2 learners benefit from already understanding events and spatial relations?
choices: They can learn new linguistic expressions for established concepts
Existing concepts eliminate the need to learn new grammatical mappings
General knowledge guarantees that L1 representations cannot interfere
The learner can acquire L2 only by memorizing complete translations
why: Existing conceptual knowledge reduces some demands. The remaining linguistic mappings can still require substantial reorganization.

stem: When does reusing an L1 representation count as negative transfer?
choices: When it obscures a distinction required by L2
Whenever prior knowledge becomes active, even if it supports the correct mapping
Only when the learner benefits from a shared meaning
Whenever the learner consciously notices a linguistic similarity
why: Transfer's effect depends on fit between systems. Activation of prior knowledge can help or hinder.

stem: English listeners map Hindi dental and retroflex stops to one familiar category. What learning problem results?
choices: Two contrastive L2 sounds are assimilated to one L1 category
The two Hindi categories must have identical acoustic properties
The listener has no established category relevant to the sounds
The difficulty concerns only producing the English word labels
why: The established category reduces the salience of an L2 distinction. Learning requires reorganizing that mapping.

stem: Why might classifiers challenge an English-speaking Chinese learner beyond remembering a new form?
choices: They require attending to noun properties not used by English in that grammatical choice
Only the pronunciation of one form, with no change in attention to nouns
A requirement to classify every object by social gender
A direct copy of English determiner choice with different vocabulary
why: The new grammar makes different semantic distinctions relevant to selecting a form.

stem: Two French synonyms have different grammatical genders. What must the learner keep separate?
choices: Grammatical class and real-world or social properties
The referents' shared meaning uniquely fixes their grammatical class
Grammatical gender can be inferred from the object's social identity
Agreement follows only word meaning, not noun-class membership
why: Gender is a grammatical classification with agreement consequences, not a direct description of an object's social identity.

stem: Why can cognates support early learning?
choices: Form similarity connects a new label with existing lexical knowledge
Similarity ensures that every associated meaning is the same
Cognates benefit only advanced learners, not initial acquisition
Useful transfer requires the same grammatical gender in both languages
why: A useful form–meaning correspondence facilitates learning. False friends show why similarity is evidence rather than certainty.

stem: A learner interprets embarazado through English embarrassed. What process produces the mistake?
choices: A familiar-looking form activates an inappropriate L1 meaning
The new form is processed without activating any known representation
The error demonstrates a failure of all transfer rather than a misleading mapping
The L2 word necessarily has the English meaning despite its use
why: The association is compelling but misleading. Negative lexical transfer can arise from a generally useful similarity bias.

stem: Why use invented foreign-like forms in paired-associate learning?
choices: Their similarity to known Dutch words can be manipulated systematically
The pairs reproduce fully known foreign words rather than new learning
Similarity can be tested only after participants become fluent
The design holds similarity fixed while changing only retention delay
why: Controlled new forms let researchers test acquisition from the start, with defined similarity and concreteness factors.

stem: Cognate-like pairs show faster acquisition and better week-later recall. What does that pattern support?
choices: Similarity benefits both initial learning and retention
Similarity helps recognition but cannot contribute to initial learning
Delayed retention is independent of how a mapping was acquired
Only the immediate receptive response supports a benefit
why: The immediate and delayed comparisons address different stages. Benefits across them extend beyond one recognition guess.

stem: Why is generating a new form more diagnostic than only recognizing its familiar meaning?
choices: It reduces the explanation that transparent similarity alone allowed guessing
It eliminates all differences between cognate and noncognate items
It supplies the unfamiliar form directly and asks for its meaning
It measures only how transparent a new form looks
why: Productive testing requires retrieval of the learned form. Receptive cognate meanings can sometimes be inferred without that mapping.

stem: A table has both concreteness and cognate advantages. Why should those effects not be collapsed?
choices: They are separate manipulated item properties
Concrete meanings necessarily make every item a cognate
The delay changes cognate status into concreteness
The two effects are different labels for one manipulation
why: Concrete/abstract meaning and similar/dissimilar form are distinct dimensions. Each can contribute to learning and forgetting.

stem: What defines an onset cohort competitor?
choices: A word compatible with the target's initial spoken material
A word related to the target's meaning without onset overlap
Any picture that resembles the target object visually
Only the target's direct translation regardless of sound overlap
why: Shared onset evidence temporarily activates multiple lexical candidates; later sounds can distinguish them.

stem: Why can matches compete with English speaker for Russian–English listeners?
choices: Its Russian name overlaps with the English input
The English names of the pictured objects share their onset
Speaker and matches are semantic synonyms
The task requires a conscious decision to translate the target
why: The overlap is cross-language and phonological. The picture makes activation of the other language observable in the task.

stem: In English, Russian-name competitors attract looks above control even beside an English competitor. What follows?
choices: Task language does not fully restrict early activation to English
The Russian object must become the final selected target
An English competitor prevents all simultaneous Russian activation
The result establishes equal competitor strength in every display
why: The result supports cross-language competition during L2 processing, while relative competitor strength still varies with the display.

stem: The English competitor's small advantage in the Russian task is not statistically reliable. How should it be summarized?
choices: No reliable cross-language competitor effect was detected there
The small numerical gap proves a reliable effect equal to L2 competition
The result establishes exactly zero activation for every learner and task
The reverse-language condition is theoretically redundant
why: Absence of a reliable observed effect is not a precise universal zero. The reported asymmetry is still theoretically informative.

stem: Which configuration explains stronger L1 influence during L2 in the illustrated model?
choices: Stronger L2-to-L1 links and stronger L1 conceptual connections
Identical lexical and conceptual links for all levels of experience
Completely separate conceptual stores without cross-language routes
A requirement that L2 concepts always become stronger than L1 concepts first
