why: The Revised Hierarchical Model uses asymmetric connections shaped by learning and experience.

stem: Why does balanced bilingualism not necessarily mean two isolated monolingual systems?
choices: Strong conceptual access in both languages can sustain cross-language competition
Balance guarantees no competitor activates in the nonrequired language
Stronger shared access removes the need for any inhibitory control
The model predicts two fully independent systems whenever proficiency matches
why: Stronger access can increase interaction. The model motivates control demands rather than guaranteeing a universal cognitive advantage.

stem: Korean adoptees perform like monolingual French listeners on tested Korean contrasts. What is established?
choices: No residual discrimination advantage was detected on those tasks
The task proves every possible early representation was erased permanently
Their early acquisition history therefore could not have included Korean
The test directly establishes that later relearning cannot show an advantage
why: The observation concerns accessible performance in specified tasks. Relearning can test different consequences of early exposure.

stem: Why compare ongoing language exposure when contrasting adoptees and childhood overhearers?
choices: Maintenance opportunities can affect whether early representations remain accessible or aid relearning
The groups differ only in the language named on the test
Early exposure has the same retention consequences regardless of later input
A negative initial test guarantees identical outcomes after retraining
why: Input history, family context, transfer, and later learning opportunities all change the relevant experience.

stem: What does Lenneberg's cerebral-dominance account propose as relevant to a learning window?
choices: Developmental changes in language lateralization
The direct strengthening of every grammatical rule through formal schooling
A capacity preserved completely by early use regardless of later maturation
A change in vocabulary size used as the definition of hemispheric dominance
why: The proposal links maturation and hemispheric organization to learning capacity. A language test does not directly measure lateralization itself.

stem: Why are L2 learners useful for age-of-acquisition research?
choices: They provide many onset ages in people with an established language
They provide randomized onset ages with all exposure quality matched
They remove transfer by including an already acquired L1
Their prior language makes task design irrelevant
why: The population is broader than rare delayed-L1 cases, but its experience and language-pair variation still require consideration.

stem: What does ultimate attainment refer to in Johnson and Newport's question?
choices: The proficiency eventually measured after learning experience
The speed of acquiring the first few words
The participant's age rather than a proficiency outcome
The closing time of a neural window measured independently of language
why: Ultimate attainment differs from initial learning speed and from a direct neural measure.

stem: Participants hear sentences and judge grammaticality without time pressure. Which source of knowledge can this particularly encourage?
choices: Explicit rule reflection
Only spontaneous implicit processing under conversational speed
Articulatory ability without grammatical knowledge
The amount of speech heard independently of response strategy
why: An untimed judgment permits conscious monitoring, so it can draw on metalinguistic knowledge as well as fluent language knowledge.

stem: Why examine early and late arrival ranges separately instead of quoting one overall correlation?
choices: A slope in one range can coexist with broad nonsloping variability in another
The overall correlation independently identifies a discrete closing event
The early and late ranges must have identical within-group slopes
Each range measures a different language rather than onset age
why: The form of the relationship matters. A single summary can hide age-dependent differences in the pattern.

stem: What does nearly random late-arrival accuracy mean in the lecture's scatterplot description?
choices: Accuracy varies without a clear relationship to AOA within that range
All participants in the late group answered the sentences randomly
Late learners produced the same low score regardless of individual differences
The points show a precise additional decline with every later arrival year
why: The randomness refers to the relation between age and attainment in the later group, not necessarily random responding.

stem: Which finding forms part of Johnson and Newport's early-arrival pattern?
choices: Often near-native accuracy for the earliest learners
Uniform chance accuracy in all childhood arrivals
No difference between the earliest and latest childhood arrivals
An identical attainment score for every learner arriving before puberty
why: Earlier attainment is often high and declines across later childhood onset. The later group shows wider variability.

stem: Why does the sensitive-period interpretation attend to both an early slope and later scatter?
choices: It proposes developmental decline followed by more individual-dependent learning
It predicts that every adult has precisely the same low final score
It treats later scatter as proof that language exposure stopped
It explains age patterns without any assumptions about learning capacity
why: The explanation links pattern shape to a change in learning determinants, rather than only comparing average scores.

stem: Under the exercise hypothesis, what should early successful L1 acquisition protect?
choices: Further language-learning capacity against decline from nonuse
A fixed native vocabulary size independent of continued experience
Equal attainment for all language pairings regardless of transfer
Preserved capacity only for the original language and no possible later language
why: The exercise proposal makes preserved later capacity conditional on early use. Maturational-state decline does not require prior nonuse.

stem: Older learners have an early L1 yet show lower L2 attainment. Which hypothesis is more directly compatible?
choices: Maturational-state decline despite early exercise
Complete preservation of subsequent acquisition ability through early use
A lack of any first language in the older learners
An explanation based only on never exercising language in childhood
why: The key contrast is whether early exercise preserves child-like subsequent learning. These learners did exercise an L1.

stem: A learner explains an English rule correctly but struggles in spontaneous use. What distinction is illustrated?
choices: Explicit metalinguistic knowledge versus fluent implicit use
Receptive vocabulary versus productive vocabulary with identical access demands
A grammatical representation versus no linguistic knowledge whatsoever
A difference explained solely by the printed forms of words
why: Knowing a rule consciously and using it automatically are not identical task accomplishments.

stem: Untimed GJT scores correlate strongly with years of formal L2 education. Why does that matter?
choices: School-based explicit learning may contribute to the measured attainment
The test directly measures maturation without any schooling contribution
The correlation establishes that arrival age is irrelevant to every task
Formal instruction supplies a measure of implicit fluency alone
why: The association supports considering explicit knowledge in this task. It does not by itself eliminate maturation or other influences.

stem: Why might Spanish–English learners differ from Chinese/Korean–English learners at similar arrival ages?
choices: The available transfer depends on the language pairing
Age alone fixes identical outcomes regardless of the prior language
Every tested English construction has an equivalent L1 mapping
A language pair changes only pronunciation and never grammar learning
why: Similarity and differences between linguistic systems change the task of learning English.

stem: Late learners handle questions relatively well although children acquire them late in L1. What idea is weakened?
choices: L2 necessarily repeats the same construction order as L1 development
Different constructions can have different transfer support
A total attainment score pools distinct grammatical structures
Older learners bring prior representations to a new language
why: An L2 learner has a different starting system. The order can reflect transfer and task demands rather than a replay of infant acquisition.

stem: Why might English determiners be especially difficult for a learner whose L1 lacks that system?
choices: The learner must acquire distinctions not already organized similarly in L1
The difficulty must be explained only by global hearing acuity
A missing L1 equivalent makes the English construction unlearnable
The absence of determiners in L1 has no effect on attention to the pattern
why: An absent corresponding system changes what must be learned and attended to, giving transfer a construction-specific role.

stem: A different L1 group shows a different AOA–attainment distribution. What must a broad maturational explanation also address?
choices: How language pairing and transfer affect the observed relationship
The same arrival age guarantees equivalent experience and test knowledge
A single downward overall correlation proves a language-pair-independent mechanism
The changed group automatically invalidates every earlier age observation
why: A successful account must connect age-related claims with population and language-pair differences rather than treating one pattern as universal.

stem: Why is arrival age not automatically a pure measure of maturational capacity?
choices: It can covary with amount, quality, and context of experience
It is the same measure as years of formal education by definition
It directly records the brain's capacity independently of exposure
It guarantees identical amount and quality of input after arrival
why: An observed timing relation can involve several mechanisms. Experience history must be distinguished from biological maturation.

stem: Two tests yield different age relationships: untimed judgment and spontaneous conversation. What is the most productive interpretation?
choices: Their different demands may draw on different mixtures of knowledge
All tests measure the same knowledge with the same processing demands
One result must be discarded because any task difference is irrelevant
Untimed judgment necessarily measures only implicit competence
why: Task design changes the balance of monitoring, explicit knowledge, and fluent use. The contrast can clarify what an age effect concerns.

stem: Which summary is best supported by the L2-sensitive-period material?
choices: Earlier learning often helps, while constructions, tests, transfer, and experience affect attainment
An early advantage requires adults to learn more slowly in every initial lesson
Any adult success eliminates the possibility of a sensitive-period effect
One distribution establishes an absolute postpubertal inability to acquire grammar
why: The synthesis preserves the observed earlier advantage while identifying mechanisms and measurements that change its interpretation.

stem: How does late-L2 difficulty after an early L1 change a simple reading of delayed-L1 evidence?
choices: It suggests early exercise alone may not preserve all later learning capacity
It proves late first-language deprivation has no lasting effects
It establishes identical developmental histories for late L1 and late L2 learners
It shows every grammatical construction declines at the same rate
why: The exercise and maturational-state hypotheses make different predictions for learners who already had a language. The L1/L2 comparison helps separate them.
